active_paradigms.idea: Replace full-coordinate basin search with a symmetry-quotient active-contact solve using arbitrary-precision mpmath.findroot
active_paradigms.description: The current program is successful because it correctly optimizes the diameter-normalized formulation, uses analytic SLSQP derivatives, and then removes much of the residual with a KKT root solve. Its principal weakness is that it searches 39 free coordinates with rotational gauge freedom and infers contacts through a tolerance, so tiny changes in the selected contact graph or residual feasibility can determine the final 1e-5-level result. Start from the current incumbent once during development, build its lower- and upper-contact colored graph, and identify vertex orbits under color-preserving graph automorphisms. Parameterize one coordinate representative per orbit, imposing the corresponding rotations/reflections explicitly, rather than retaining all 14 independent positions. Write only the distinct lower-distance, upper-distance, and stationarity equations in that quotient parameterization and solve them directly with high precision using mpmath.findroot. Convert the resulting coordinates to float64 only at return time, normalize by the actual float64 maximum pdist-equivalent distance, and retain the candidate only if its directly recomputed float64 ratio exceeds the stored incumbent. This is fundamentally a structural reduction rather than another stochastic search: it should identify whether the apparent optimum is an exact symmetric extremizer and eliminate the numerical drift that limits the current program.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: The primary squared ratio, especially elimination of diameter-contact residuals and improvement beyond the reference caused by a more accurate realization of the same extremal contact graph.
active_paradigms.cautions: Do not use the raw SLSQP contact tolerance as the mathematical graph definition; inspect gaps between distance levels and retain only contacts stable under several tolerances. Fix translation, rotation, and scale in the quotient equations, otherwise findroot sees singular gauge directions. The returned float64 geometry, not the high-precision internal residual, is what must be scored, so perform a final float64 rescale and direct all-pairs validation.

active_paradigms.idea: Use rigidity-matrix SVD to distinguish a truly rigid optimum from a flexible active-set branch before choosing equations
active_paradigms.description: The current KKT polish assumes every pair within 3e-5 of a boundary belongs to one fixed contact graph, then uses Levenberg--Marquardt despite the unavoidable rotational nullspace. That can solve an overinclusive or rank-deficient graph and explains why further full-space restart effort is unlikely to yield reliable improvement. Form the signed rigidity/KKT Jacobian at the best candidate using lower contacts, upper contacts, and the derivative with respect to the minimum squared distance. Apply scipy.linalg.svd to this matrix and inspect singular vectors after removing the six Euclidean similarity gauge directions. If there is an additional near-null direction, it is a real feasible flex of the active graph: perturb specifically along that vector, choosing the sign that increases slack on noncontacts while preserving active equalities to first order, rather than using isotropic Gaussian perturbations. If no such direction exists, use the SVD-derived left null vector as the equilibrium stress certificate and prune contacts with near-zero or wrong-sign stress; the remaining stressed graph is the one appropriate for an exact solve or hardcoded construction. This makes the search contact-graph aware and attacks the actual limitation of the present method, namely ambiguous active sets, rather than repeating failed global continuous optimization methods.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Primary ratio through discovery of a higher-ratio neighboring contact topology or through removal of spurious active constraints that artificially pin the present local solution.
active_paradigms.cautions: Distance constraints at the lower and upper boundary have opposite signs in the stress equations, and valid multipliers must obey the corresponding nonnegative KKT signs. Explicitly project out three translations, three rotations, and scale if diameter is not fixed; otherwise ordinary gauge singular values will be mistaken for useful flexes. Treat SVD as a deterministic structural test, not as a score by itself, and reject any flex whose full pairwise distances violate a formerly inactive bound.

active_paradigms.idea: Derive and return a compact algebraic orbit construction, with polynomial roots chosen by numpy.roots instead of runtime nonlinear optimization
active_paradigms.description: After the colored contact graph has been stabilized, attempt to express the 14 vertices as a small union of geometric orbits, such as antipodal pairs and cyclic/reflection orbits around an axis. The promising evidence is that a 14-point diameter extremizer near the benchmark is likely governed by a highly constrained two-distance contact structure; the current repulsion plus SLSQP pipeline is expensive largely because it rediscovers this structure numerically on every evaluation. Express squared distances between each orbit type as polynomials in a few radii, heights, and cosine values, set the identified lower contacts to u and upper contacts to one, and eliminate all but one scalar parameter offline. Solve its univariate polynomial with numpy.roots, select the real root that satisfies every inequality with the greatest directly evaluated float64 ratio, and generate the 14 coordinates from the associated orbit formula. The final submitted function should contain this deterministic construction and optionally a precomputed selected root/coordinates, not the seed search, 108 SLSQP calls, or tolerance-dependent KKT graph detection. Such an algebraic realization is also the most reliable way to preserve a small gain over the benchmark across evaluator machines and timeout budgets.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: The same sole evaluator scalar, with emphasis on exact equality of the true minimum and maximum distance levels after float64 rounding and deterministic reproducibility.
active_paradigms.cautions: Do not assume antipodality or a named polyhedron without verifying all 91 distances: an attractive symmetric seed can be below the current optimized result. When selecting roots, evaluate reconstructed Cartesian coordinates in float64 because cancellation can change which pair is the maximum. Keep a known-good stored coordinate fallback if no real root passes all inequalities, since polynomial elimination can introduce extraneous branches.

tried_paradigms.idea: Replace stochastic basin hopping with a symmetry-reduced global search using scipy.optimize.differential_evolution
tried_paradigms.description: The current program first performs spherical inverse-power repulsion, then applies many SLSQP solves to the full 39-coordinate constrained problem. Its strength is the correct diameter-one formulation with analytic derivatives, which reaches the apparent reference contact graph; its principal weakness is that SLSQP is local and the many random perturbations mostly revisit the same basin. Instead, encode a plausible high-symmetry 14-point orbit construction with only a few geometric parameters, such as ring radii, heights, angular offsets, and any distinct orbit representatives under a chosen finite rotation/reflection group. Evaluate the true squared ratio directly after centering and scaling by the candidate diameter, so no separate scale variable or upper-distance constraints are needed. Call scipy.optimize.differential_evolution once on the bounded reduced parameter vector, with a fixed seed, Sobol initialization, polishing enabled, and tight tolerances. The optimizer should search several symmetry classes in separate program variants, rather than treating a single full-coordinate local optimum as evidence that its contact graph is globally best. This is especially promising because the score is already within numerical noise of the benchmark, so identifying the exact symmetry family can remove small asymmetries and expose a better contact configuration.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: The sole target is the evaluator's squared ratio (minimum pairwise squared distance divided by maximum pairwise squared distance). Reducing dimension makes global topology/contact-graph changes more likely than the current perturb-and-SLSQP schedule.
tried_paradigms.cautions: The construction must always emit exactly 14 finite points; avoid parameterizations that merge orbit points at zero radius. The objective is nonsmooth when the identity of a shortest or diameter pair changes, so use a sufficiently large population and do not infer success from a smoothed surrogate alone. A symmetry restriction can miss an asymmetric optimum, so use several independently motivated orbit parameterizations as alternative submitted programs, not sequential optimizations in one call.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use a contact-graph equation solve with scipy.optimize.least_squares to obtain an exact rigid candidate
tried_paradigms.description: The current code already reveals the useful principle: after diameter normalization, the optimum is governed by a small set of active lower-distance contacts and active diameter pairs, while most of its 182 inequalities are slack. Its weakness is that SLSQP repeatedly handles all inequalities and can terminate with small residual violations or an imprecise, slightly asymmetric realization of the same active graph. Build a fixed candidate contact graph from the near-reference configuration: include pairs repeatedly attaining the minimum distance, pairs attaining the diameter, and enough additional contacts to make the framework rigid after fixing translation, rotation, and scale. Parameterize the 14 coordinates in a gauge-fixed form and use scipy.optimize.least_squares once to solve residual equations d_ij^2-u=0 for short contacts and d_ij^2-1=0 for diameter contacts, with optional residuals enforcing intended symmetry. Start from a fixed, hard-coded numerical approximation of the known candidate rather than conducting a preceding optimizer run. After the solve, return the coordinates directly and let the evaluator compute the actual extrema; inactive pairs then certify whether this contact graph is feasible and superior. This attacks numerical error and contact degeneracy rather than merely launching more random full-dimensional searches.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Exact equalization of the distance classes that determine dmin and dmax, thereby improving the true squared ratio and reducing loss from SLSQP feasibility tolerances.
tried_paradigms.cautions: least_squares is an equation solver, not a global maximizer: the selected graph must be independently feasible and rigid, and every noncontact pair must be checked after solving. Fix a complete Euclidean gauge, for example point 0 at the origin, point 1 on the x-axis, point 2 in the xy-plane, plus one diameter normalization, or the Jacobian will be rank deficient. Do not force all near-short pairs to equality if the intended optimum requires some of them to be slack.

tried_paradigms.idea: Directly optimize the normalized max-min objective with scipy.optimize.dual_annealing in gauge-fixed coordinates
tried_paradigms.description: The existing implementation is a hybrid of spherical-code seeding, constrained local SQP, and many incumbent perturbations. This works because spherical repulsion provides well-separated points and analytic constraints make local polishing efficient, but it is biased toward spherical seeds and has no mechanism for accepting a temporary score decrease needed to change the nearest-neighbor graph. Use a gauge-fixed coordinate vector for 14 unrestricted 3D points, with translation removed and a fixed overall box large enough to contain a diameter-one realization. Define one scale-invariant objective as the negative of min(d2)/max(d2), computed from all 91 squared distances, and add deterministic tiny tie-breaking only if needed for numerical stability. Make exactly one scipy.optimize.dual_annealing call with a fixed seed, broad but justified coordinate bounds, high visit parameter, and a local search option using its built-in polishing facility. Unlike the constrained formulation, this has no feasibility boundary: every noncoincident configuration has a valid score, and annealing can cross changes in which pair realizes the diameter or minimum. A successful result can reveal a distinct contact topology; it is then also a source of a fixed candidate for a later equation-based construction, though that later step should be in a separate program variant.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Global improvement of the actual evaluator quantity, including moves that alter both the minimum-distance contact graph and the diameter graph simultaneously.
tried_paradigms.cautions: The ratio is undefined at collapsed configurations, so return a large finite penalty whenever max(d2) is tiny or any value is nonfinite. Bounds should only fix gauge and numerical scale; they must not impose an artificial unit-cube geometric restriction. Full 36-dimensional annealing may be costly, so combine it with a fixed symmetry-aware or gauge-reduced parameterization when timeout is tight, and always use a fixed random seed.

tried_paradigms.idea: Replace the repeated SLSQP basin search with one high-accuracy interior-point solve using scipy.optimize.minimize(method="trust-constr") on the diameter-normalized formulation.
tried_paradigms.description: The current program first produces spherical-code seeds by repulsion, then performs many SLSQP solves of the correct epigraph problem: maximize u subject to u <= d_ij^2 <= 1. This is strong because it directly matches the evaluator's squared ratio, fixes translation, supplies analytic first derivatives, and uses restarts to cross some contact-graph basins. Its main limitation is that SLSQP's active-set decisions and finite termination can leave a near-optimal configuration slightly inside or outside the true diameter/contact manifold; the observed 1.000016 score is consistent with a nearly correct known optimum rather than a clearly better geometry. Use scipy.optimize.minimize once with method="trust-constr", the same 39 coordinate variables plus u, exact lower and upper squared-distance constraints, and a scipy.optimize.NonlinearConstraint with the existing analytic Jacobian. Provide a Hessian update strategy such as BFGS or SR1, use very small barrier and optimality tolerances, and remove rotational null directions by fixing point 0 at the origin, point 1 on the x axis, and point 2 in the xy plane. Start from one deterministic high-quality seed rather than using the incumbent from a succession of optimizers. The interior-point trajectory can approach a degenerate active-contact solution more reliably than SLSQP, while the final u is exactly the evaluator metric after diameter normalization.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: The sole target is u=(dmin/dmax)^2. In particular, reduce numerical slack in simultaneously active minimum-distance and diameter constraints, since improvement over the reference is likely at the 1e-5 level.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Do not maximize unsquared distance or constrain only a selected subset of pairs: all 91 lower and all 91 upper constraints must remain present. Gauge fixing must be implemented consistently in the variable unpacking and Jacobian. Return the coordinates and let the evaluator recompute distances; do not return the optimizer's u. trust-constr may need a realistic execution budget and sparse Jacobian representation to avoid timeout.

tried_paradigms.idea: Solve the rigid active-contact equations directly with scipy.optimize.least_squares, using a fixed contact graph of the known 14-point diameter extremizer and KKT stationarity residuals.
tried_paradigms.description: A qualitatively different route is to treat the best configuration as a tensegrity/contact-graph realization rather than as a generic inequality NLP. The current spherical repulsion plus SLSQP is good at discovering an approximate basin, but it does not exploit that at an optimum many pairs are exactly at the minimum distance or exactly at the diameter, and the remaining coordinates are determined to high precision by those equalities. Identify a fixed candidate contact graph from a trusted high-precision 14-point extremal configuration: label each edge as a short contact with d_ij^2=u or a diameter contact with d_ij^2=1. In one scipy.optimize.least_squares call, solve residuals consisting of these edge equations, translation/rotation gauge equations, and the KKT force-balance equations with nonnegative multipliers for the two edge classes. Include u, coordinates, and multipliers as variables, with bounds enforcing u>0 and nonnegative multipliers. The overdetermined residual system makes the geometric realization and its equilibrium self-stress much more stable than trying to infer active constraints afresh at every iterate. Evaluate all 91 distances afterward; if every noncontact distance lies strictly between u and 1, this produces a highly precise feasible candidate and can expose whether the reference's tiny excess is merely numerical. This directly targets the local algebraic optimum rather than attempting more random basins.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Numerical precision of the extremal contact geometry and verification that noncontact pairs do not become the true dmin or dmax. This is especially appropriate when the current score already nearly matches a known reference bound.
tried_paradigms.cautions: This requires the contact graph to be correct; an incorrect graph can solve its equalities beautifully while violating an omitted pairwise bound. Do not derive the graph dynamically by running another optimizer inside the submitted function; hard-code a graph and a deterministic initial realization. Include enough gauge constraints to eliminate the six Euclidean rigid-motion degrees of freedom, and explicitly reject a result if any of all 91 distances violates its assigned interval.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.optimize.differential_evolution as a single global search over a symmetry-reduced, smooth soft-extrema objective to seek a genuinely different contact graph.
tried_paradigms.description: The present method's biggest global-search weakness is that all its seeds are spherical repulsion configurations and all subsequent moves are local SLSQP perturbations of one incumbent; this strongly favors the same spherical-code contact topology. Form a direct objective for scipy.optimize.differential_evolution over symmetry-reduced coordinates, fixing translation and rotation as point 0=(0,0,0), point 1=(x,0,0), and point 2=(a,b,0). For each candidate, center and scale it internally by its largest pairwise distance, then maximize a differentiable lower approximation to the minimum squared distance, for example a log-sum-exp soft minimum with a high inverse temperature over all 91 normalized squared distances. This normalization makes bounds on coordinates practical and exactly removes scale from the search objective. Use Sobol initialization, deterministic seed, workers=1, polish=False, and a population budget chosen for the timeout; this is a single global optimization call rather than a repulsion stage followed by local polishing. At the end, compute the exact hard min/max ratio only to select the returned member of the final population, not as a second optimization stage. Unlike an inequality solver, this approach can discover a different combinatorial contact graph whose actual hard ratio exceeds the apparent reference value.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Global exploration of contact-graph topology and the exact evaluator ratio, with the smooth surrogate used only to rank candidates during the one search call.
tried_paradigms.cautions: A soft minimum can favor a candidate with many moderately short pairs instead of the best hard minimum; use a sufficiently sharp temperature and validate the exact ratio before return. Coordinate bounds must be broad enough not to exclude an equivalent realization, while gauge fixing avoids wasting dimensions on translations and rotations. Differential evolution can be expensive in 33-plus dimensions, so it is a topology-discovery alternative, not something to combine with the current repeated SLSQP pipeline.

tried_paradigms.idea: Recover the incumbent’s active contact graph and solve its exact KKT/contact equations with scipy.optimize.root
tried_paradigms.description: The current program is a diameter-normalized continuous nonlinear program: spherical repulsion supplies a seed, then SLSQP maximizes the lower squared-distance variable under all 91 lower and upper distance inequalities, with noisy restarts used to cross nearby basins. Its strength is the correct scale-free formulation and analytic constraint Jacobian; its weakness is that SLSQP terminates at a tolerance-limited active-set point and does not explicitly impose the algebraic equalities defining the final contact graph. Run the current method once offline, identify pairs whose squared distances are within a tight threshold of the attained minimum or maximum, and hard-code that graph plus a gauge fixing translation, rotation, and scale. Form a square system consisting of active lower contacts equal to u, active diameter contacts equal to 1, and stationarity equations with nonnegative contact multipliers for the max-u problem. Use scipy.optimize.root with method='lm' or method='hybr' on this fixed system from the hard-coded numerical solution. Return only the reconstructed coordinates, after checking all inactive pairs remain strictly between u and 1. This is fundamentally a rigidity/KKT polishing method rather than another stochastic global search, and can remove the few-ppm numerical discrepancy left by inequality SLSQP.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: The actual squared ratio dmin^2/dmax^2, particularly precision at the known near-optimal contact topology rather than evaluator time.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Do not use scipy.optimize.least_squares, which was already unsuccessful. The selected active equations must be independent after gauge fixing; include multipliers and stationarity rather than merely forcing too many pair distances equal. Root solving is local, so the contact graph and starting coordinates must be extracted offline from the successful incumbent, and the returned result must be independently checked against all 91 pairs.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use a symmetry-orbit template and globally certify its low-dimensional parameters with scipy.optimize.shgo
tried_paradigms.description: The present repulsion-plus-SLSQP code searches 39 free coordinate variables and is therefore prone to finding only one numerical realization of a highly symmetric diameter graph. Inspect the successful configuration’s distance matrix for identical distance signatures, partition its 14 vertices into geometric orbits, and encode the corresponding reflections, rotations, or antipodal relations as an explicit coordinate template. The template should leave only a small number of radii, heights, twist angles, and perhaps one axial separation as variables; fix the diameter analytically or retain explicit pairwise upper constraints. Optimize u directly subject to every template pair satisfying u <= squared_distance <= 1 using one scipy.optimize.shgo call with Sobol sampling and a sufficiently large sampling budget. SHGO is viable only after this symmetry reduction, because it triangulates/bounds a low-dimensional parameter box rather than attempting a 39-dimensional global search. It can discover a competing contact topology or establish that the incumbent’s observed symmetry family has no higher feasible ratio. This differs from the failed differential evolution and annealing trials because the decisive change is an exact geometric dimension reduction, not a different random global optimizer in unconstrained coordinates.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: The primary squared ratio, by exploring globally across discrete contact-graph transitions that local SLSQP restarts may miss.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Do not run SHGO on all 42 raw coordinates; that is intractable. The orbit template must be derived from actual distance/signature evidence rather than assumed from a spherical code, since the optimum is not required to lie on a sphere. Bound angular variables carefully, remove equivalent rotations/reflections, and recompute dmin/dmax from the final 14 expanded points rather than trusting the auxiliary u.

tried_paradigms.idea: Perform a discrete diameter-packing feasibility search over a symmetry-adapted candidate library with scipy.optimize.milp
tried_paradigms.description: Treat the problem as a finite approximation to a diameter-one packing problem rather than as a smooth optimization problem. Construct offline a large deterministic candidate library concentrated near the successful configuration’s convex hull, its apparent symmetry orbits, and small structured perturbations of its vertices; retain the library as constants in the submitted program. For a target squared separation slightly above the current value, build one binary MILP: select exactly 14 candidates, and add x_i+x_j<=1 for every candidate pair whose squared distance is below the target or above 1. Solve that single feasibility/selection model with scipy.optimize.milp and return the selected candidates if it finds a 14-set. The current continuous approach is strong at obtaining coordinates but weak at deliberately changing the contact combinatorics; this formulation searches those combinatorics exactly within the candidate library. It is particularly useful as an independent route to identify a different feasible diameter graph, after which the selected coordinates can themselves be hard-coded if they beat the incumbent. Unlike failed continuous global optimizers, integrality prevents the search from drifting through infeasible near-contact arrangements.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Feasibility of a threshold above the current dmin^2/dmax^2 and discovery of alternative discrete contact patterns; evaluator time is secondary.
tried_paradigms.cautions: A plain Cartesian grid will be far too coarse to beat a ppm-level incumbent, so candidates must be symmetry-adapted and locally refined offline. This is a fixed-threshold, single MILP call in the evaluated function; avoid an in-function threshold bisection or a subsequent continuous optimizer. Include both forbidden-too-close and forbidden-over-diameter pair edges, use sparse scipy constraints, and verify the chosen 14 points contain no duplicate candidate indices.
